transcription.tex: \textbf{Mechanics Year 1 · Chapter 11}\par \textbf{Variable Acceleration}\par Functions of time\par Differentiation and turning points\par Integration and distance travelled
\[v=\frac{ds}{dt},\qquad a=\frac{dv}{dt}.\]\par Integrate in the reverse direction, using initial conditions to find the constants.

transcription.tex: 1. A particle has velocity \(v=\tfrac12t^3\) m/s. Find its velocity after 4 s, and the time when \(v=108\) m/s.\par 2. Another particle has \(v=2t^2-16t+24\), for \(t\ge0\). Find:\par a. initial velocity;\par b. times at rest;\par c. time when \(v=64\);\par d. greatest speed on \(0\le t\le5\).
1. \(v(4)=32\) m/s.\[108=\tfrac12t^3\Rightarrow t=6\text{ s}.\]
d. Check endpoints and \(v\)’s turning point:\[v(0)=24,\]\[v(4)=-8,\]\[v(5)=-6.\]\par Greatest speed \(=24\) m/s.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 6. A particle starts at the origin with velocity \(v=8t-2t^2\) m/s, \(t\ge0\).\par a. When is it next instantaneously at rest?\par b. Find its greatest speed on \(0\le t\le4\).
a. \(2t(4-t)=0\). The next time is \(t=4\) s.
b. Velocity is non-negative throughout the interval.\[\frac{dv}{dt}=8-4t=0\Rightarrow t=2.\]\par \(v(2)=8\) m/s; both endpoint velocities are zero. Greatest speed: 8 m/s.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 7. A particle leaves \(O\) and later returns to \(O\). Its distance from \(O\) is modelled by\[s=3t^2-t^3,\quad0\le t\le T.\]\par The model is valid while \(s\ge0\). Find \(T\) and explain.
\[s=t^2(3-t).\]\par The non-zero root is \(t=3\). For \(t>3\), the expression becomes negative and cannot represent distance.
The particle returns to \(O\) at \(T=3\) s. The stated distance model ends there.

b. \(4t^3-32=0\Rightarrow t=2\) s.

transcription.tex: A cat’s displacement from a house is\[s=t^3-\tfrac32t^2-36t\text{ m},\quad t\ge0.\]\par a. Find its velocity at \(t=2\).\par b. When is it at rest?\par c. Find its acceleration at \(t=5\).
b. \((t+3)(t-4)=0\). Reject negative time: \(t=4\) s.

transcription.tex: A yo-yo’s distance below the hand is\[s=0.6t+0.4t^2-0.2t^3,\quad0\le t\le3.\]\par a. Justify the time restriction.\par b. Find the maximum distance from the hand to 3 s.f.
a. \(s=\tfrac15t(3-t)(1+t)\). It is non-negative for \(0\le t\le3\), returning to the hand at \(t=3\).
b. \(v=0.6+0.8t-0.6t^2=0\).\[t=\frac{2+\sqrt{13}}3=1.8685\ldots\]\par The other root is negative. Substitution gives maximum distance 1.21 m.

transcription.tex: 5. A particle starts at \(O\); its distance from \(O\) is\[s=\tfrac92t^2-t^3,\quad0\le t\le4.5.\]\par a. Sketch its displacement–time graph.\par b. Justify the restriction.\par c. Find its greatest distance from \(O\).\par d. Find the acceleration magnitude there.
a–b. \(s=t^2(4.5-t)\): starts with a horizontal tangent at \((0,0)\), rises to a maximum, then returns to \((4.5,0)\). Beyond 4.5 s it is negative, so cannot represent distance.
c. \(v=9t-3t^2=3t(3-t)\).\par The maximum occurs at \(t=3\): \(s=13.5\) m.
d. \(a=9-6t\). At \(t=3\), \(a=-9\) m/s², magnitude 9 m/s².

transcription.tex: 6. A train moves along a straight 4 km test track. Its displacement from the start is modelled by\[s=3.6t+1.76t^2-0.02t^3.\]\[0\le t\le90.\]\par Show that it never reaches the far end of the track.

Velocity changes from positive to negative at \(59.672\) s, giving the maximum.\[s_{\max}=2230\text{ m (3 s.f.)}<4000\text{ m}.\]\par The train never reaches the end. Negative later displacement means it has passed the starting point in the opposite direction.

transcription.tex: \textbf{Using integration}\[v=\int a\,dt,\qquad x=\int v\,dt.\]\par Use initial conditions to find each constant.\par A particle has \(v=6t-t^2\), \(t\ge0\), and \(x(0)=5\).\par a. Find \(x(t)\).\par b. Find its distance from its starting position at \(t=6\).
b. \(x(6)=41\), so distance from starting position is \(|41-5|=36\) m.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A particle has velocity \(v=5-3t^2\) m/s, \(t\ge0\). Find the distance travelled in the third second of its motion.
The third second is \(2\le t\le3\). Velocity is negative throughout this interval, so distance is the negative of displacement.
\[\Delta s=\int_2^3(5-3t^2)\,dt=[5t-t^3]_2^3\]\[=-12-2=-14\text{ m}.\]\par Distance travelled: 14 m.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: A particle has \(v=2t^2-9t+4\) m/s and \(x(0)=15\) m.\par a. Find the times at rest.\par b. Find acceleration at \(t=5\).\par c. Find total distance travelled on \(0\le t\le5\).

c. Integrate: \(x=\tfrac23t^3-\tfrac92t^2+4t+15\).\par Velocity changes sign at both rest times. Add the three positive distances:\[\tfrac{23}{24}+\tfrac{343}{24}+\tfrac{25}{6}=\tfrac{233}{12}\text{ m}.\]

transcription.tex: 8. A particle starts at \(O\) with velocity\[v=6t^2-26t+15\text{ m/s}.\]\par Find the two non-zero times when it passes through \(O\).
\[x=t(2t-3)(t-5)=0.\]\par Excluding \(t=0\), it passes through \(O\) at 1.5 s and 5 s.

transcription.tex: 9. A particle starts at \(O\) with velocity\[v=3t^2-12t+5\text{ m/s}.\]\par a. When does it return to \(O\)?\par b. Find the distance travelled on \(2\le t\le3\).
b. Velocity is negative throughout \([2,3]\); its zeros are approximately 0.473 and 3.528.\[x(2)=-6,\qquad x(3)=-12.\]\par Distance: \(|-12-(-6)|=6\) m.

transcription.tex: 10. A particle has acceleration \(a=4t-3\) m/s² and initial velocity 4 m/s. At \(t=T>0\), its velocity is again 4 m/s. Find \(T\).
\[v=2t^2-3t+C.\]\par Initial velocity gives \(C=4\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: \textbf{Constant acceleration formulae}\par A particle has constant acceleration \(a\), initial velocity \(u\), and initial displacement zero. Use integration to prove:\par a. \(v=u+at\);\par b. \(s=ut+\tfrac12at^2\).
a. \(v=\int a\,dt=at+C\).\par At \(t=0\), \(v=u\), so \(C=u\).\[v=u+at.\]
b. \(s=\int(u+at)\,dt=ut+\tfrac12at^2+K\).\par At \(t=0\), \(s=0\), so \(K=0\).\[s=ut+\tfrac12at^2.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX draft; explicit question/answer objects

transcription.tex: 3. Prove that \(s=ut+\tfrac12at^2\), with \(u,a\) constant, describes constant acceleration \(a\).\par 4. Which displacement functions have constant acceleration?\par A. \(s=2t^2-t^3\)\par B. \(s=4t+7\)\par C. \(s=t^2/4\)\par D. \(s=3t-2/t^2\)\par E. \(s=6\)
3. \(v=u+at\), then \(dv/dt=a\), a constant.
4. Differentiate twice:\par A. \(4-6t\): not constant.\par B. \(0\): constant (uniform velocity).\par C. \(1/2\): constant.\par D. \(-12/t^4\): not constant.\par E. \(0\): constant (stationary).
